mcqs.question: In the Observer-pattern design of this notification system, why doesn't the dispatcher branch on 'if channel is email, do X; if SMS, do Y'?
options: Observer pattern requires all observers to behave identically
The dispatcher only ever supports a single channel at a time
Branching on channel type is handled by the UserPreference class instead
Each channel is an independent observer that decides for itself whether and how to act when notified, so channel-specific logic lives inside each observer, not the subject
mcqs.explanation: The whole point of Observer here is that the subject (the event) stays ignorant of what any observer does with the notification — that knowledge is encapsulated inside each channel implementation. The dispatcher supports many channels simultaneously; UserPreference filters which channels apply but doesn't contain per-channel send logic; and Observer specifically allows dissimilar observer behavior, not identical.

mcqs.question: Why can't Notification.send() produce a single DeliveryStatus field once channels can fail independently?
options: One notification fans out into N independently-tracked delivery attempts, one per (notification, channel) pair, and different channels can legitimately be in different states — delivered on email, failing and retrying on SMS — at the same time
Because DeliveryStatus objects cannot be stored in a database
Because templates render differently for each channel
Because channels must all succeed or all fail together for the notification to count as sent
mcqs.explanation: Independent failure per channel means the true state of a notification is a set of per-channel statuses, not one value — collapsing them into a single field would hide, for example, an SMS retry loop behind a successful email send. This has nothing to do with database storage or template rendering, and channels explicitly do not need to succeed or fail as a unit.

mcqs.question: A notification's first send attempt actually succeeds, but the confirmation is delayed and a retry fires anyway. How does the design prevent the user from being notified twice?
options: By disabling retries entirely once a notification is created
By deduplicating on a stable (notification id, channel) key, checked before sending, so a retry after a slow-but-successful attempt finds the key already marked sent and becomes a no-op
By sending all retries through a different channel than the original attempt
By requiring the user to manually dismiss duplicate notifications
mcqs.explanation: Idempotency here comes from checking a stable dedupe key before every send, including retries — if that key is already marked sent, the retry does nothing further. Disabling retries would break legitimate failure recovery; switching channels or relying on the user to dismiss duplicates doesn't solve the underlying double-send problem at all.

mcqs.question: Why does queue-based fan-out isolate a slow notification channel better than push-based (synchronous) fan-out?
options: Queue-based fan-out doesn't require a Template renderer
Push-based fan-out cannot support more than one channel at a time

In queue-based fan-out, the dispatcher enqueues a per-channel job and returns immediately, so a slow channel's backlog builds up in its own queue without blocking the dispatcher or other channels; push-based fan-out blocks the caller until each channel responds in turn
Queue-based fan-out guarantees zero message loss under any failure
mcqs.explanation: The isolation comes specifically from decoupling the dispatcher's return from each channel's actual completion — a queue lets a slow channel back up on its own without stalling the caller or other channels. Both approaches still need per-channel templates and both support multiple channels; queue-based reduces blast radius but doesn't by itself guarantee zero loss (that still depends on retry and durability design).

mcqs.question: Why is it a mistake to mark a notification 'delivered' as soon as the channel provider's API returns a 200 response?
options: A 200 response only means 'accepted for delivery,' not that the user actually received it — an email can still bounce or a push token can be stale, and collapsing 'sent' and 'delivered' hides those real failures from anything depending on delivery outcome
A 200 response is never returned by real notification providers
It causes the dispatcher to stop sending to all other channels
It prevents the Template renderer from formatting the message correctly
mcqs.explanation: The gap between provider acceptance and actual user receipt is exactly where real failures hide if the two states are conflated. Providers do return 200s routinely; this doesn't affect other channels' dispatch or template rendering — the issue is specifically that downstream logic (like preference-based fallback) loses visibility into genuine delivery failures.
